title: The art of dying
hookLine: medieval handbooks taught how to die well: with faith, forgiveness and company

lines: DEMONS ON ONE SIDE, ANGELS ON THE OTHER.
cards: A man lies in bed, and the room is crowded. In the old woodcuts, small demons crouch on the blanket, holding up scrolls of temptation: you've done too much wrong, it's too late, hold on to your money.
On the other side, angels lean in, and saints stand at the bedside. The man barely moves; everything happens around him, and all of it is about him.
The pictures come from little handbooks made in medieval Europe and passed from hand to hand, so ordinary people, not only priests, would know what to do when someone was dying.

teach.b: Ars moriendi means the art of dying. It sounds grim, but the handbooks were trying to be kind. First, it was practical.
A priest might not arrive in time, so the books told friends and family what to say and do. Nobody was supposed to die alone; company was part of the art. Second, the temptations.
The books named the fears that come at the end, among them despair: the thought that it's too late for mercy. Their answer came from the Gospels.
One of the men crucified beside Jesus, with nothing left to offer, says, "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." Jesus answers, "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise."
If it wasn't too late for him, the books said, it isn't too late for you. Third, forgiveness: settle what you can, ask pardon and give it.
The model again was the cross, where Jesus prays, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."

teach.h: YOU LEARN IT BY LIVING IT.
teach.b: Fourth, the turn: you can't learn an art on the last day. The handbooks were read by the healthy too. To forgive at the end, practice forgiving now; to trust at the end, practice trusting on a Tuesday.
Dying well, they thought, is mostly the shape of how you lived. Christians still keep pieces of this.
Catholic and Orthodox families may call a priest for anointing and last prayers; Protestant families may gather to read scripture and pray at the bedside. The tools differ.
The idea is the same: nobody should face it unready, or alone.

how: In Catholic and Orthodox churches a priest may be called to anoint and pray with the dying; in Protestant churches a pastor and family may gather at the bedside to read scripture, pray and say goodbye.

games.q: you're the man crucified beside Jesus. you have nothing left to offer and almost no time. what do you say?
o: "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom."
"if you're the Christ, save us both."
games.why: he asks to be remembered, and Jesus answers, "to day shalt thou be with me in paradise." the handbooks used this scene against despair.

practice: Let one grudge come up, not the biggest in your life, a medium one you've carried longer than it deserves, and for this minute try loosening your hold on it.

If you pray, you can use the words from the cross, Father, forgive them; if not, simply let your grip loosen a little. If despair ever feels close, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Ars moriendi. Latin for the art of dying: old handbooks teaching faith, forgiveness and company at the end of a life.

orig.note: Latin: ars, art or skill; moriendi, of dying.

carryVoice: Your line: die well, live well. The art is learned on ordinary days. Go gently.
